display.purpose: The skill name or heading at the head of the block; 40px on narrow screens.

count.purpose: The number on the reversed plate, and nowhere else.

title.purpose: The headings of the lesson, the problem, and the verdict.

body.purpose: Prose, captions, and the answer box, capped at 60ch; tabular figures.

body-row.purpose: Phrasings (italic) and dates in the rail, so nine rows fit the 1080 frame.

label.purpose: The margin list and the plate's caption; key letters at weight 800.

label-small.purpose: The privacy line; margin notes take its size and leading at weight 500.

apparatus.purpose: Tracked uppercase margin headings, standing in for small caps.

label-nav.purpose: The top navigation's text: 700, 18px, 1.2; the product name inside it is 900, 20px.

label-stamp.purpose: Framed small labels: the demo-data label, the end rule, and the verdict's returned stamp: 700, 16px, 1.3.

display-narrow.purpose: The display heading at 67.5rem and below: 40px.

motion.name: drop-duration
motion.purpose: One rail key's drop into its detent.

motion.name: drop-step
motion.purpose: Delay between successive keys, in date order across the year cut; nine keys seat in 840ms.

motion.name: drop-ease
motion.purpose: A critically damped spring: it rises to rest and never passes it. The key falls from translate 0 -120%; none under reduced motion or on a returned card.

breakpoints.name: narrow
breakpoints.purpose: At and below: one column, margin above the block, rail outboard on the left, plate in flow.

narrative.overview:
Every screen is set like a page of a wide-margin reference edition drawn by a ruling engine. A small, dense block holds the work; a wide margin around it carries the apparatus; and down the middle of the block runs one rail with a vermilion key on it for every borrow. Your own words sit on one side of the rail and what they point to sits on the other, so the keys show how often you asked before any number does.

The surface is for operating, not reading: navigation, buttons, and inputs stay the web's standard controls, and the world lends only type, palette, density, and the rail. The edition's bone stock and text serif are translated to proof gray and a grotesk, because a warm cream ground with a serif is the default look the user ruled out. Density is high and calm: one block per screen, ruled in 1px hairlines, with nothing that glows, floats, or bounces.

Motion has one grammar: a key drops into its detent along a single damped axis with no overshoot. That drop is the only orchestrated motion. It runs in date order, across the year cut, every time a borrowed card is set in the block: each key falls 120% of its height into its detent over 400ms, one 55ms step after the key before it, so nine keys are seated in 840ms. The easing is a critically damped spring written as `linear()` that never passes 1, and the detent clips the key, so nothing fades. A returned card's keys are already seated and don't drop. Under reduced motion the keys are simply in place.
keyCharacteristics: One rail per block, one vermilion key per borrow.
Proof-gray ground, white block, iron-black ink, one rubric.
One reversed black plate per screen, for the number that matters.
Square corners and 1px hairlines; no shadows and no radius.
Standard controls in the world's type, never a costume of a printed page.

rules.name: The One Rubric Rule
rules.body: Vermilion appears only on the rail's keys and the margin's key letters. On a heading, a border, a background, or a state, it's wrong.

rules.name: The One Ramp Rule
rules.body: Every neutral comes from one fixed ramp between Proof Gray and Iron Black, stepped in OKLab: Proof Gray, Hover Gray, Rule Gray, Disabled Gray, Pressed Iron, Iron Black. No one-off grays.

rules.name: The No New Ink Rule
rules.body: States add no color: a returned card's margin key is struck through in iron black, and a failed rep's verdict frame goes from 1px to 3px iron black.

rules.name: The 1080p Floor Rule
rules.body: In the demo video's 1080p frame, body text renders at 20px or more and labels and apparatus at 14px or more; size the CSS for the viewport the video records. Judges may only see the video, and one builder's rule for product videos is "body text ≥ 20px at 1080p" ([@elie2222][x-video]). The sketch's 13px and 17px sizes fall below it and don't carry over.

rules.name: The No Display Face Rule
rules.body: No display face beyond the text family, and no monospace. Apparatus stays in tracked capitals of the same family.

rules.name: The Reversed Plate Rule
rules.body: One element per screen sits on a black plate with white type: the number that matters most on that screen. A second plate means the first one isn't the point.

rules.name: The Plate Holds Rule
rules.body: Once a screen has its count, every state keeps its one plate, inside the block's padding: waiting and error too. Until then, while a screen waits for the count itself (its first load, or a file being read) or fails to get it, there's no plate, since the Plate Counts Rule leaves nothing to put on one. A plate that drops out of a short state once its count is known, such as a project's card that failed to come, or hangs past the block's foot, is wrong.

rules.name: The One Bar Rule
rules.body: Each year's rail is one continuous gray bar between two iron hairlines, and a key has no cell or frame of its own. Keys in separate gray cells read as a column of checkboxes.

dos: **Do** build from the chosen sketch and the world's [quality-bar board][board], not from adjectives; a builder's advice for avoiding the model's default look is "Steal a reference, don't describe one" ([@ArchiveExplorer][x-ref]).

**Do** keep to three signature elements: the rail, the reversed plate, and the hairlines. One designer's checklist for distinctive AI-built UI says "1–3 strong custom elements beat 20 random assets" ([@Hartdrawss][x-mood]).

**Do** take texture only from the real object, the ruling engine's hairlines. One post calls the skeuomorphism revival "already as obnoxious and overplayed" ([@PalmyrPar][x-revival]), and a reply says "we don't need AI to give a UI a paper texture and a fun font" ([@Mirteaaa][x-costume]).
**Do** keep the reversed plate's number readable at thumbnail size, and let motion settle before the next interaction, so a recording never shows half-moved state.
donts: **Don't** use a warm cream ground or a serif display face; together they're the bookish default the user ruled out.
**Don't** make it feel like an app kit: no rounded cards, soft shadows, toasts, or progress bars. The user ruled these out too.

**Don't** use the tells from a widely shared list of reasons a site "looks vibe-coded": Inter, Geist, or Space Grotesk; Lucide icons; emoji; sparkle icons; bento grids; dot grids; a colored left stripe; soft corner radius; hover animations ([@suraj_sharma14][x-vibe]).

**Don't** fade or slide sections in on load, and don't stagger reveals; "everything fading in" is the model's default look ([@ArchiveExplorer][x-ref]), even though a widely shared aesthetics prompt recommends staggered reveals ([@vincenteliezer][x-stagger]). The rail's key drop is the only orchestrated motion.
**Don't** add purple gradients, all-caps eyebrow labels above headings, or "→" on buttons ([the PRD's Avoid list](/devpost/prd.md#look-and-feel)). Apparatus lives in the margin, never as an eyebrow.

**Don't** draw streaks, flames, badges, scores, or charts. [The PRD's Avoid list](/devpost/prd.md#look-and-feel) rules out streaks, badges, scores, and charts, and one critique says Duolingo "monetizes guilt through streaks, badges & reminders" ([@StockSavvyShay][x-guilt]).
